title: One thing that Die Hard (1988) has that I feel a lot of other action movies are lacking, is that Hans Gruber’s scheme is completely believable.

commenti.body: [removed]
[removed]

Die hard was essentially a heist film from the side of a minor player (just an out of town beat cop with an ex inside) who took the plan apart one person at a time. Heist films often (not always) have believable plans. What happened is that when die hard got copied, it copied the “psychotic over the top bad guys get taken apart one by one”, not “heist film with a twist“.

Now, personally, I’ve enjoyed quite a few of the movie’s cloning or influenced by die hard. So unrealistic or not, it’s a winner for me.
[removed]

Yes and coherent villainous plans make the villain much more frightening. Because in order to evaluate his plan, to get the feeling as to whether it will work or not, to picture what the weaknesses might be, you have to imagine it. This means you have to also picture all the awful things he intends to do and see him victorious. Even if only in your mind's eye. The disturbing vision is created.

Hans Gruber is one of the most captivating and memorable villains of all time, and he's essentially just a thief.

Die Hard is amongst the best examples there is that you don't need a complex, sympathetic backstory to write a good villain.

He is somewhat likeable because of how competent he is versus how incompetent the authorities are.

And yes, they let the mask slip at particular moments such as his losing his temper with Holly, to add to the impact.

I think uncomplicated villains who are just evil for selfish reason can only work if they enjoy themselves though otherwise theyre just brutes. Hans has a lot of fun doing what he does until things truly fall apart which makes him so satisfying to watch
Hitchcock once said that if someone is good at their job, the audience will like them, even if they're criminals or horrible people.

Yes, it's not the crime that makes Gruber interesting, it's the glee and enthusiasm he has for executing it. He knows his plan is brilliant and he's pumped full of adrenaline now that it's actually happening. 

It's the stoic, emotionless, too-cool-to-be-thrilled "masterminds" that make boring villains.

>he's essentially just a thief.

He's an *exceptional* thief, u/BeefPieSoup, and since he's moving into kidnapping, you should be more polite.

> Hans has a lot of fun doing what he does until things truly fall apart which makes him so satisfying to watch

It's easy to be captivated by Rickman's Gruber, but I think it's equally key to success that, as great as Gruber is, he's just one of *many* characters in *Die Hard* that get great lines and great moments. Sure, he gets the most of them, but I think what sets *Die Hard* apart from other movies with fantastic Rickman bad-guy performances (*Quigley Down Under*, *Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves*) is that **every** character in *Die Hard* gets to steal scenes or at least do or say something cool. 

"I don't want neutral, I want dead."

"I'm Agent Johnson. This is Special Agent Johnson. No relation."

"We're going to need some more FBI guys, I guess."

Al Leong eating the candy bar. 

"Hey, what am I, a method actor?"

"You didn't bring me along for my charming personality." (and the deleted line: "although you could have.")

So much care and attention to all of the characters. Even the stock characters like henchmen or the asshole/idiot police captain get *something*. Which is only fair, I guess. It's Christmas!
He's likeable because he's charming and personable. If he wasn't trying to rob you or shoot someone you care about, you probably wouldn't have any reason to dislike him.
yeah I don't need to like them, I just need to like watching them.

I agree, but I would definitely give credit to Rickman for his role in making Gruber such an awesome character. A well written villain in the hands of a lesser actor is not going to have the same impact.

I like how Die Hard does a sort of twist with Gruber just being a thief. It initially seems like he's a West German Communist terrorist and then it's discovered that he doesn't actually care about politics at all and is just taking money. McClane is even more disgusted by this, since it means he's purely selfish rather than at least thinking he's in the right.
Isn’t that essentially a reason why we love Heat?

I read a screenwriting book^* that had a list of, I think, 12 character attributes that would make the audience like them (in the sense of wanting to follow their story). I think the author said your hero and villain had to have at least 8 or 9 of them. Interestingly, only one of the items was "being a good person." 

I'd have to look up the list, but I distinctly remember Tony Montana (Al Pacino's character in *Scarface*) checked off 11 boxes--"good" was the only thing he missed, but people still loved the character.

---

^* ^Screenwriting ^books ^are ^largely ^bullshit, ^so ^I'm ^not ^saying ^I ^subscribe ^to ^this ^theory; ^I ^just ^found ^it ^interesting.

It's a time of miracles! So be of good cheer.

And call me when you get the last lock.

I agree with everything you wrote, but I'd also add an addendum--*Die Hard* also does a good job of *explaining* the plan (and also hiding the exposition).

A lot of people complain about villains' plans not making sense, but if you give them just a little bit of thought, the plans are perfectly fine. It's the *movie* that didn't convey the plan.

Alternatively, people complain that the villain couldn't possibly have planned everything, when that is, in fact, the point. But since the movie didn't *show* the villain changing their plans mid-movie, certain audience members (and youtube critics) complain that the plan makes no sense.
pretty much any movie with a great villain. look at Hannibal Lector.

Plausibility is a funny thing in that very few types of films are really realistic, but the " car leap over a building" physics of the last 15 years have made some of the 80s movies seem documentary-ish. 

Die Hard is great in that it's more realistic for the Gruber team to enter the vault than for John Maclane to try saving the day. It makes for better stakes.

Die hard with a vengeance is arguably one of my favorite movies, it just captivated me early in life and I thoroughly enjoy rewatching it almost ritualistically every year. One thing your comment made me realize is how mcclane is surprised to find out simon is essentially just a thief ("They were after gold! and a shit load of it!"), but that really was just the family business.

And that’s what makes Hans so captivating: Alan Rickman makes sure he’s always doing something worth investing your attention. The way he moves and interacts with the environment with subtle gestures (I’m thinking of his Alexander the Great monologue to Takagi) is really a joy to watch.

die hard with a vengeance has one of, if not my favorite opening in any movie. The music opening to the bomb, to the transition to the detectives just staring at mcclane, not revealed yet, but their faces are so disgusted, to the reveal of him looking like he just crawled out of a gutter, it's perfect. "I got a headache, no i mean it really i have got a bad fuckin headache!", "hey asshole... ya got any aspirin", there's so many great lines but the fact that the script doesnt let you forget mcclane is hungover the entire plot is nothing short of amazing.

I feel like greed works better as a villain plan than “world power.” Lex Luther’s plan in Superman The Movie is to destroy CA so that his desert real estate property becomes more valuable. It’s not even believable, but it’s hilarious and simple. Goldfinger’s plan is to irradiate the gold reserve at Fort Knox so that his own gold becomes more valuable. That’s it. In fact, it’s a twist reveal that his plan isn’t any more complicated than that. I think that’s amazing.

So Hans being a bank robber instead of a terrorist works perfectly. It’s a great twist. That film has so many other things going for it as well. Hans is super charming and entertaining to watch. The doling out of his plan to the audience is done perfectly. And of course John McClain being a vulnerable all-too-human action hero was relatively novel at the time.
I would be interested to hear the other attributes, reservations about screenwriting books notwithstanding. Do you remember which one you pulled that from?

It's called *[The Story Solution](https://amzn.to/46yzTFN)*, by Eric Edson. He was a professor at CSUN, where I got my MFA. Interesting guy, bit of a kook.

I misremembered the numbers. There were *nine* attributes that create a "sympathetic response" and "bond an audience to the hero." He said you **must** include five, but six or seven is better. 

1. Courage
2. Unfair Injury
3. Skill
4. Funny
5. Just Plain Nice
6. In Danger
7. Loved by Friends and Family
8. Hard Working
9. Obsessed

I think "nice" is what I mistook for "good."

I like how he doesn't have any combat experience that makes him a major danger to John McClane. When they first met face to face and if McClane knew who he was talking to the movie would have been over.

It feels like in general the first installment of action movies are usually grounded before the sequels go comepletely insane but Rambo sticks out to me personally. First Blood was just a skilled military vet surviving in the wilderness while on the run from local cops. By Rambo 3, he was literally a shirtless maniac running around Afghanistan taking out an entire countries army by himself.
